name: Deep Sea Logistics
background: A shipping company needs to transport a sequence of containers across the ocean. The containers are loaded onto a ship one by one in the exact order they arrive at the dock. The ship makes a fixed number of trips, and on each trip, it can carry any number of containers as long as their total weight does not exceed the ship's capacity.
task: Given a list of container weights in arrival order and the maximum number of trips allowed, find the minimum possible weight capacity the ship must have to complete the job within the trip limit. The ship must carry at least one container per trip unless all containers are already delivered.
input_format: Line 1: Two integers N and D, representing the number of containers and the maximum number of trips. Line 2: N space-separated integers representing the weight of each container in order.
constraints: N is between 1 and 100,000. D is between 1 and N. Each weight is between 1 and 10,000.

name: The Master Binder
background: A publisher is binding a massive series of historical documents into a set of physical volumes. To maintain the narrative flow, the documents must remain in their original chronological order. Each volume has a maximum page limit, and the publisher wants to minimize this limit while ensuring the entire series fits into a specific number of volumes.
task: Given the page counts of N documents in order and the maximum number of volumes K, determine the smallest possible maximum page capacity per volume required to bind all documents.
input_format: Line 1: Two integers N and K. Line 2: N space-separated integers representing the page count of each document.
constraints: N is between 1 and 200,000. K is between 1 and N. Document pages are between 1 and 10^9. The total sum of pages will not exceed 2^63 - 1.

name: Stream Buffer Optimization
background: A video streaming service sends data in discrete segments. To prevent lagging, segments are grouped into 'bursts'. The hardware can process a limited number of bursts per second. Each burst has a maximum data size (capacity). To optimize network stability, the service wants to find the smallest possible burst capacity that still allows all segments to be sent within the burst count limit.
task: Given N segment sizes in their transmission order and a maximum number of bursts M, calculate the minimum burst capacity needed.
input_format: Line 1: Two integers N and M. Line 2: N space-separated integers representing the size of each segment.
constraints: N is between 1 and 100,000. M is between 1 and N. Segment sizes are between 1 and 10^6.

name: Precision Assembly
background: An automated factory processes items on a conveyor belt. Items arrive in a fixed sequence, and each takes a specific amount of time to process. The factory operates in shifts. During one shift, the assembly line processes a contiguous block of items. The total time taken in any single shift cannot exceed the line's time-capacity.
task: Given the processing times for N items and a limit of S shifts, find the minimum time-capacity required for the assembly line to complete all items within the shift limit.
input_format: Line 1: Two integers N and S. Line 2: N space-separated integers representing the processing time for each item.
constraints: N is between 1 and 150,000. S is between 1 and N. Processing times are between 0 and 10^5.

name: Server Batch Processing
background: A cloud provider has a queue of jobs that must be processed in the order they were submitted. Each job requires a specific amount of memory. The provider allocates a set of servers, where each server handles a contiguous sequence of jobs from the queue. All servers are configured with the same memory capacity.
task: Given the memory requirements of J jobs and the available count of K servers, find the minimum memory capacity each server must have to ensure all jobs are processed.
input_format: Line 1: Two integers J and K. Line 2: J space-separated integers representing the memory requirement of each job.
constraints: J is between 1 and 200,000. K is between 1 and J. Memory requirements are between 0 and 10^9.

name: Router Range
background: You have a list of possible one-dimensional positions (integers) where routers may be mounted along a line. You must place exactly k routers at those positions. The 'minimum separation' is the smallest difference between any two chosen router coordinates. We want to make that smallest gap as large as possible. If k > n (more routers than available positions) there is no solution.
task: Given n candidate integer coordinates and an integer k, choose exactly k of the coordinates to maximize the minimum pairwise distance between any two chosen coordinates. If k <= 1 the minimum separation is defined to be 0. If no solution exists (k > n) output -1. Otherwise output a single integer: the maximum achievable minimum separation.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers n and k
Line 2: n integers x1 x2 ... xn (space-separated positions, any order)
constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; positions xi are 32-bit signed integers (|xi| <= 1e9); 1 <= k <= 200000. Expected O(n log range) solutions.

name: Checkpoint Arrangement
background: You are placing exactly k checkpoints at some of the given one-dimensional positions. The goal is to maximize the minimum distance between any two checkpoints. If several placements achieve the same optimum, return the placement produced by the left-to-right greedy choice: sort positions ascending and always pick the earliest available position that preserves the required gap when building the placement for the final optimal gap.
task: Given n candidate coordinates and an integer k, find the maximum possible minimum separation D between k chosen coordinates. If k <= 1 define D = 0. If k > n output a single line with -1. Otherwise output two lines: first line the integer D, second line the k chosen coordinates in ascending order produced by the specified greedy tie-breaking.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers n and k
Line 2: n integers x1 x2 ... xn (space-separated positions, any order)
constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; coordinates xi are integers with |xi| <= 1e9; 1 <= k <= 200000.

name: Stadium Seating Feasibility
background: You are given candidate seat coordinates and must check whether it is possible to seat exactly k people so that every pair of seated people are at least D units apart. If k <= 1 this is always considered possible. Seats may share coordinates (duplicates).
task: Given n coordinates, integers k and D (D >= 0), output YES if it is possible to select exactly k of the given positions so that the minimum pairwise distance between chosen positions is at least D; otherwise output NO. If k > n output NO.
input_format:
Line 1: three integers n, k and D
Line 2: n integers x1 x2 ... xn (space-separated positions, any order). D is a non-negative integer.
constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; 0 <= D <= 2e9; coordinates xi are integers with |xi| <= 1e9; 1 <= k <= 200000.

name: Sensor Indices
background: Sensors can be installed only at given discrete coordinates; each candidate has a fixed original input index. You must choose exactly k candidates to maximize the minimum distance between any two chosen sensors. When coordinates tie, treat candidates with the same coordinate but different original indices separately. To make output deterministic, sort candidates by (coordinate, original index) and run the standard left-to-right greedy. Finally report the indices (1-based original positions) of the selected candidates, listed in increasing numerical order.
task: Given n coordinates in the order they were provided and an integer k, if k > n output -1. Otherwise compute the maximum achievable minimum distance D (if k <= 1 then D = 0). Then, using the sorted tie-breaking described, pick k coordinates that realize D and output two lines: first line D, second line the k chosen original 1-based indices in ascending numeric order.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers n and k
Line 2: n integers x1 x2 ... xn (space-separated positions, in their original input order)

name: Lighthouse Placement
background: Along a straight coast there are candidate integer mile markers where lighthouses can be built. You must build exactly k lighthouses at those markers. Maximize the minimum distance between any two lighthouses. If multiple placements achieve the same optimal minimum distance, the placement that starts furthest to the left (smallest first lighthouse coordinate) is preferred; return that first coordinate to break ties. If k > n there is no solution.
task: Given n mile-marker coordinates and integer k, if k > n output -1. Otherwise output two lines: first the maximum achievable minimum separation D (define D = 0 if k <= 1), second the coordinate of the first (leftmost) lighthouse for the leftmost-optimal placement described above.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers n and k
Line 2: n integers x1 x2 ... xn (space-separated positions, any order)

name: The Gluttonous Gourmet
background: A food critic is tasked with sampling several plates of snacks before a festival begins. The critic eats at a constant integer speed of 'K' snacks per hour. Once the critic starts a plate, they must finish it before moving to the next. If a plate has fewer snacks than the critic's hourly speed, they still spend the full hour finishing that plate and do not start the next one until the next hour begins.
task: Given a list of snack counts on each plate and a deadline in hours, find the minimum integer speed K (snacks per hour) such that the critic can finish all plates within the deadline.
input_format:
Line 1: Two space-separated integers, N (number of plates) and H (deadline in hours).
Line 2: N space-separated integers representing the number of snacks on each plate.

name: Server Bandwidth Allocation
background: A server needs to download a series of files. The server can only download one file at a time. The download speed is fixed at an integer rate of R megabits per second (Mbps). For any file, the time taken is the file size divided by R, rounded up to the nearest second, because the server only initiates new transfers at the start of a second.
task: Determine the minimum integer rate R (Mbps) required to complete all downloads within T seconds.
input_format:
Line 1: Two space-separated integers, N (number of files) and T (total time limit in seconds).
Line 2: N space-separated integers representing the size of each file in megabits.

name: Quality Control Quota
background: A quality control technician inspects batches of circuit boards. The technician works at a fixed integer rate of B boards per minute. Each batch must be completed before starting the next. If a batch is finished in the middle of a minute, the technician waits until the start of the next minute to begin the next batch.
task: Find the minimum integer rate B (boards per minute) to finish inspecting all batches within M minutes.
input_format:
Line 1: Two space-separated integers, N (number of batches) and M (total time in minutes).
Line 2: N space-separated integers representing the number of boards in each batch.

name: Speed Reading Challenge
background: A student needs to read several chapters of a textbook. The student reads at a constant integer speed of P pages per hour. A chapter must be finished entirely before the student can start the next one. If a chapter ends partway through an hour, the student takes a break and starts the next chapter at the beginning of the next hour.
task: Calculate the minimum integer speed P (pages per hour) required to read all chapters within K hours.
input_format:
Line 1: Two space-separated integers, N (number of chapters) and K (total hours available).
Line 2: N space-separated integers representing the number of pages in each chapter.

name: Electric Fleet Charging
background: A fleet of electric vehicles is lined up at a charging station. The station charges one vehicle at a time at a constant integer rate of W kilowatts (kW). Charging time is calculated as the energy needed (kWh) divided by the rate W, rounded up to the nearest hour. The next vehicle cannot start charging until the current hour is finished.
task: Find the minimum integer charging rate W (kW) to ensure all vehicles are charged within H hours.
input_format:
Line 1: Two space-separated integers, N (number of vehicles) and H (total hours available).
Line 2: N space-separated integers representing the energy required by each vehicle in kWh.
constraints: 1 <= N <= 200,000; N <= H <= 1,000,000,000; Energy requirements are between 1 and 1,000,000,000.

name: Lecture Blocks
background: You have a sequence of lecture durations (nonnegative integers). You must cut the sequence into contiguous blocks (each block contains consecutive lectures) so that there are exactly k blocks. The objective is to minimize the largest total duration among the blocks. If it is impossible to make exactly k non-empty blocks, report -1.
task: Given n and k and an array of n nonnegative integers, partition the array into exactly k contiguous, non-empty groups. Output the minimum possible value of the largest group sum. If no partition into exactly k non-empty groups exists (i.e., k>n), output -1. Ties are resolved by the numeric minimum of the largest sum.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers n k
Line 2: n space-separated nonnegative integers a1 a2 ... an
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000, 1 ≤ k ≤ 200000, 0 ≤ ai ≤ 10^9, O(n log(sum ai)) expected.

name: Shard Logs At-Most
background: You need to split a stream of log sizes (nonnegative integers) into at most k contiguous shards. You may use fewer than k shards. The objective is to minimize the maximum shard sum. When the same minimal maximum can be achieved by several shardings, choose the solution that uses the smallest possible number of shards (still ≤ k) and report that number along with the minimal maximum.
task: Given n and k and an array of n nonnegative integers, partition the array into at most k contiguous groups. First minimize the largest group sum; among all partitions achieving that minimal maximum, output that minimal maximum and the smallest number of groups used. Always produce two integers: the minimal possible largest group sum and the minimal number of groups achieving it.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers n k
Line 2: n space-separated nonnegative integers a1 a2 ... an
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000, 1 ≤ k ≤ 200000, 0 ≤ ai ≤ 10^9. Greedy feasibility / binary search solution fits time limits.

name: Divide Pages with Minimum Chapters
background: You have a sequence of page counts for sections (nonnegative integers). You must split the sequence into exactly k contiguous chapters, and each chapter must contain at least L sections (L≥1). The goal is to minimize the largest chapter page total. If the constraints on sizes make an exact k-partition impossible, report -1.
task: Input n, k, L and the array of n nonnegative integers. Partition into exactly k contiguous groups, each group containing at least L elements. Output the minimal possible largest group sum, or -1 if no valid partition exists. If multiple partitions tie, return the numeric minimal largest sum.
input_format:
Line 1: three integers n k L
Line 2: n space-separated nonnegative integers a1 a2 ... an
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000, 1 ≤ k ≤ 200000, 1 ≤ L ≤ n, 0 ≤ ai ≤ 10^9. If k*L > n then no solution.

name: Shard Files with Max-Count
background: You have files of nonnegative sizes in a given order. Each shard may contain at most M files (contiguous in the original order). You may use up to k shards in total (you may use fewer). The objective is to minimize the maximum shard size. If respecting the per-shard element limit makes it impossible to fit into k shards, report -1.
task: Given n, k, M and an array of n nonnegative integers, partition the array into at most k contiguous groups where each group contains at most M elements. Output the minimal possible largest group sum, or -1 if no valid partition exists (i.e., if ceil(n/M) > k).
input_format:
Line 1: three integers n k M
Line 2: n space-separated nonnegative integers a1 a2 ... an

name: Cargo Trucks Allow Empty
background: You must load n cargo items (nonnegative weights) in the given order into exactly k trucks. Trucks are filled as contiguous blocks of items; however, trucks are allowed to be empty. The objective is to minimize the maximum total weight carried by any truck. Because empty trucks are allowed, it is always possible to have exactly k groups (k≥1).
task: Given n and k and an array of n nonnegative integers, partition the array into exactly k contiguous groups, where empty groups are permitted. Output the minimal possible largest group sum. Ties are resolved by numeric minimum of the largest sum.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers n k
Line 2: n space-separated nonnegative integers a1 a2 ... an
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000, 1 ≤ k ≤ 200000, 0 ≤ ai ≤ 10^9. Empty groups allowed (groups may have zero elements).

name: Wall-Break Shortest Route
background: A grid cell marked 0 is open and 1 is blocked. You may turn one blocked cell into an open cell while walking, but may move only up, down, left, or right.
task: Print the fewest moves from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, using at most one wall break. Print -1 if unreachable. Use the stated rule exactly.
input_format:
Line 1: R C.
Lines 2 through R+1: C characters 0 or 1 per row.
constraints:
1 <= R,C <= 1000
start and target are open
use at most one wall break

name: Wall-Break Shortest Route Planner
background: A grid cell marked 0 is open and 1 is blocked. You may turn one blocked cell into an open cell while walking, but may move only up, down, left, or right.
task: Print the fewest moves from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, using at most one wall break. Print -1 if unreachable. Treat all values as part of one ordered scenario.
input_format:
Line 1: R C.
Lines 2 through R+1: C characters 0 or 1 per row.
constraints:
1 <= R,C <= 1000
start and target are open
use at most one wall break

name: Wall-Break Shortest Route Checkpoint
background: A grid cell marked 0 is open and 1 is blocked. You may turn one blocked cell into an open cell while walking, but may move only up, down, left, or right.
task: Print the fewest moves from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, using at most one wall break. Print -1 if unreachable. Report the defined result without extra text.
input_format:
Line 1: R C.
Lines 2 through R+1: C characters 0 or 1 per row.
constraints:
1 <= R,C <= 1000
start and target are open
use at most one wall break

name: Wall-Break Shortest Route Tracker
background: A grid cell marked 0 is open and 1 is blocked. You may turn one blocked cell into an open cell while walking, but may move only up, down, left, or right.
task: Print the fewest moves from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, using at most one wall break. Print -1 if unreachable. Keep the required tie rule unchanged.
input_format:
Line 1: R C.
Lines 2 through R+1: C characters 0 or 1 per row.
constraints:
1 <= R,C <= 1000
start and target are open
use at most one wall break

name: Wall-Break Shortest Route Verifier
background: A grid cell marked 0 is open and 1 is blocked. You may turn one blocked cell into an open cell while walking, but may move only up, down, left, or right.
task: Print the fewest moves from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, using at most one wall break. Print -1 if unreachable. Use the same input and output rules.
input_format:
Line 1: R C.
Lines 2 through R+1: C characters 0 or 1 per row.
constraints:
1 <= R,C <= 1000
start and target are open
use at most one wall break

name: Nearest Charger Grid
background: You have a rectangular city grid. Cells are free '.' , chargers 'C', or impassable walls '#'. Time/distance is number of orthogonal steps. If a cell has a charger its distance is 0. Walls (and any cell that cannot be reached from any charger) are reported as -1.
task: For every cell output the minimum number of steps to reach any charger (0 for charger cells). Report -1 for walls or cells with no path from any charger. If multiple chargers reach a cell at the same distance, that distance is the answer.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers R C (rows and columns)
Next R lines: each a string of length C with characters in {'.','#','C'}
constraints: 1 ≤ R,C; R*C ≤ 300000. Grid only contains characters '.', '#', 'C'. Output R lines with C space-separated integers.

name: Rotting Fruit Minutes
background: Each cell holds an item: 0 = empty (no item), 1 = fresh fruit, 2 = rotten fruit. Every minute, rotten fruits rot any orthogonally adjacent fresh fruits (but do not pass through empty cells).
task: Return the minimum minutes until no fresh fruits remain. If there are no fresh fruits initially return 0. If some fresh fruits can never be rotten (no initial rotten can reach them) return -1.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers R C
Next R lines: C integers (0,1,2) separated by spaces
constraints: 1 ≤ R,C; R*C ≤ 300000. Each grid value is 0,1,2. Output a single integer.

name: Fire Spread Times on a Graph
background: An unweighted undirected graph of N nodes. Fire starts at several source nodes simultaneously. Every minute a burning node spreads fire to all its neighbors. If a node never receives fire it is considered SAFE.
task: For each node 1..N output the earliest minute it burns (0 for source nodes), or the word SAFE if unreachable from every source. If the source list contains duplicates treat them as a single start (time 0).
input_format:
Line 1: two integers N M
Next M lines: two integers u v (1-based edge endpoints)
Next line: integer S (number of sources)
Next line: S integers (source node indices)
constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 300000, 0 ≤ M ≤ 300000. 1 ≤ u,v ≤ N. 0 ≤ S ≤ N. Graph edges are undirected, no weights. Output N lines each either an integer ≥0 or the exact token SAFE.

name: Last Flooded Cells
background: Given a grid with water sources 'W', empty '.' and impassable obstacles 'X'. Each minute water spreads orthogonally to neighboring empty cells (not into obstacles). Water sources are already flooded at time 0.
task: If every empty cell is reachable from at least one water source, output two integers T K on the first line where T is the maximum minute any empty cell becomes flooded and K is the number of cells that achieve minute T. Then output K lines with 1-based row and column of each such cell, sorted lexicographically by row then column. If there are zero empty cells output "0 0" and no further lines. If some empty cell is not reachable from any water source print exactly the line IMPOSSIBLE.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers R C
Next R lines: each a string of length C using characters {'.','X','W'}
constraints: 1 ≤ R,C; R*C ≤ 300000. Water spreads only into '.' cells. Output described above exactly.

name: Nearest Hospital Queries
background: An undirected unweighted city road graph. Some nodes host hospitals. For many query nodes you must report distance (number of edges) to the nearest hospital (0 if the node itself is a hospital). If no hospital is reachable report -1.
task: Given the graph, hospital set, and a list of query nodes, output one integer per query: minimum distance to any hospital, or -1 if unreachable. Sources (hospital nodes) are simultaneous multi-source starts.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers N M
Next M lines: u v edges (1-based)
Next line: integer H
Next line: H integers (hospital node indices)
Next line: integer Q
Next line: Q integers (query node indices)
constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 300000, 0 ≤ M ≤ 300000. 0 ≤ H ≤ N. 1 ≤ Q ≤ 300000. Output Q lines each an integer ≥0 or -1.

name: The Chromatic Courier
background: In the city of Prismatica, roads are colored either Red (0) or Blue (1). To prevent driver fatigue, the city council mandates that every route must strictly alternate between Red and Blue roads.
task: Find the shortest path from intersection 1 to intersection N. The path must alternate colors, meaning if you just traversed a Red road, the next must be Blue, and vice versa. The first road taken can be either color. If multiple paths exist, output the minimum number of roads used. If no such path exists, output -1.
input_format: Line 1: Two integers N (number of intersections) and M (number of roads). Next M lines: Three integers u, v, and c, representing a road between u and v of color c (0 for Red, 1 for Blue). Roads are bidirectional.

name: Portal Duality
background: A research facility contains rooms connected by two types of portals: Alpha (0) and Beta (1). To maintain molecular stability, a traveler must alternate between Alpha and Beta portals at every step.
task: Determine the minimum number of portals required to travel from room 1 to room N. The first portal used can be of either type, but every subsequent portal must be the opposite type of the one immediately preceding it. If room N is unreachable under these conditions, output -1.
input_format: Line 1: Two integers N (rooms) and M (portals). Next M lines: Three integers u, v, and t, representing a bidirectional portal between rooms u and v of type t (0 for Alpha, 1 for Beta).

name: Robot Protocol
background: A maintenance robot moves between stations using two different gear modes: Push (0) and Pull (1). The robot's internal logic requires it to switch modes after every single movement to prevent mechanical overheating.
task: Calculate the fewest number of moves for the robot to get from station 1 to station N. The robot can start with either a Push or a Pull move. If it is impossible to reach station N while strictly alternating modes, output -1.
input_format: Line 1: Two integers N (stations) and M (connections). Next M lines: Three integers u, v, and g, representing a bidirectional connection between stations u and v using gear mode g (0 for Push, 1 for Pull).

name: Luminous Labyrinth
background: A cave system consists of chambers linked by passages that are either Light (0) or Dark (1). To keep your eyes adjusted, you must never walk through two passages of the same lighting condition in a row.
task: Find the shortest route from chamber 1 to chamber N such that the lighting condition of the passages alternates at every step. You may begin with either a Light or a Dark passage. If no such route exists, output -1.
input_format: Line 1: Two integers N (chambers) and M (passages). Next M lines: Three integers u, v, and L, representing a passage between chambers u and v with lighting L (0 for Light, 1 for Dark).

name: Bipartisan Bridge
background: In a social network, connections between users are labeled as either Formal (0) or Informal (1). A specific communication protocol requires that messages must alternate between Formal and Informal links to be verified.
task: Find the minimum number of links needed to send a message from user 1 to user N. The message must alternate link types at every hop, starting with either type. If user N cannot be reached via an alternating path, output -1.
input_format: Line 1: Two integers N (users) and M (links). Next M lines: Three integers u, v, and k, representing a bidirectional link between users u and v of type k (0 for Formal, 1 for Informal).

name: Perimeter of the Largest Island
background: You have a rectangular grid of 0/1 cells. A component (island) is any group of 1-cells connected orthogonally (up/down/left/right). The perimeter of a component is the total number of cell edges that face outside the grid or face a 0-cell.
task: Find the island(s) with the largest area (number of 1-cells). If there are no 1-cells print 0. If multiple islands tie for largest area, choose the tied island that has the largest perimeter. Output that island's perimeter.
input_format:
Line 1: H W
Lines 2..H+1: each a string of W characters '0' or '1'
constraints: 1 ≤ H, W, H*W ≤ 200000. Grid contains only '0' and '1'.

name: Perimeter at a Point
background: Given a grid of 0/1 cells, any connected group of 1-cells is a component. The perimeter of a component counts edges where a 1-cell meets the outside or a 0-cell. You are given a cell coordinate and must report the perimeter of the component that contains that cell.
task: If the query cell contains 1, output the perimeter of its component. If the query cell contains 0, output -1.
input_format:
Line 1: H W
Lines 2..H+1: each a string of W characters '0' or '1'
Line H+2: r c (1-based row and column of the queried cell)
constraints: 1 ≤ H, W, H*W ≤ 200000. 1 ≤ r ≤ H, 1 ≤ c ≤ W. Grid contains only '0' and '1'.

name: Count Components with Perimeter ≤ K
background: Each connected group of 1-cells has a perimeter (edges adjacent to outside or 0). You are asked how many components have perimeter at most K.
task: Output the number of components whose perimeter is ≤ K. If K < 0, output 0.
input_format:
Line 1: H W
Lines 2..H+1: each a string of W characters '0' or '1'
Line H+2: K (integer)
constraints: 1 ≤ H, W, H*W ≤ 200000. Grid contains only '0' and '1'. K fits in 32-bit signed integer.

name: Minimal Perimeter Among Border-Touching Components
background: A component touches the border if any of its cells lies on the first/last row or first/last column. Perimeter counts edges adjacent to outside or to 0-cells.
task: Find the minimal perimeter among components that touch the grid border. If no component touches the border, print -1.
input_format:
Line 1: H W
Lines 2..H+1: each a string of W characters '0' or '1'
constraints: 1 ≤ H, W, H*W ≤ 200000. Grid contains only '0' and '1'.

name: Sum of Perimeters of Top M Components by Area
background: Compute each component's area (number of 1-cells) and perimeter. Sort components by area descending; break ties by smaller perimeter first. Take the first M components in this order and sum their perimeters.
task: Given M, output the sum of perimeters of the selected components. If M ≤ 0 output 0. If there are fewer than M components, sum all components.
input_format:
Line 1: H W
Lines 2..H+1: each a string of W characters '0' or '1'
Line H+2: M (integer)
constraints: 1 ≤ H, W, H*W ≤ 200000. Grid contains only '0' and '1'. M fits in 32-bit signed integer.

name: Can All Courses Be Finished?
background: You have N courses numbered 1..N. A prerequisite a b means course a must be completed before course b. A valid plan repeatedly takes any course that has no remaining prerequisites and completes it. Duplicate prerequisite lines in the input should be treated as a single prerequisite. A self-loop (a prereq from a course to itself) makes completion impossible.
task: Decide whether it is possible to finish all courses by repeatedly removing courses with zero outstanding prerequisites. If it is possible print YES; otherwise print NO. Duplicate edges in the input are ignored; self-loops count as a cycle and make completion impossible.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers N M (number of courses and number of prerequisite pairs).
Next M lines: two integers a b each meaning a must be done before b.

name: One Valid Course Order (smallest-first)
background: Courses are numbered 1..N and a pair a b means a must be completed before b. You must output one valid order of all courses or report impossibility. When multiple courses have no outstanding prerequisites at the same time, always choose the smallest-numbered course next. Ignore duplicate prerequisite lines (they do not add extra requirements). A self-loop makes completion impossible.
task: If a full ordering exists, print N integers on one line: a valid course completion order following the smallest-first tie rule. If impossible, print IMPOSSIBLE exactly. Duplicate edges are ignored; self-loops make it impossible.
input_format:
Line 1: two integers N M.
Next M lines: a b meaning a before b.

name: Recipe Preparation Sequence (one per line)
background: You are preparing a recipe of N steps numbered 1..N. Each line a b means step a must be completed before step b. Produce one valid sequence of steps, printing one step per line. When several steps are available simultaneously, always take the smallest-numbered step next. Treat repeated identical prerequisite lines as a single requirement. Self-dependencies are invalid and make a full sequence impossible.
task: Print N lines with a valid ordering of steps (one integer per line) following the smallest-first rule, or print IMPOSSIBLE if no full ordering exists. Duplicate edges are ignored; self-loops cause impossibility.
input_format:
Line 1: N M
Next M lines: a b meaning a before b.

name: Build Order for Modules (comma-separated)
background: You have N modules numbered 1..N. Dependency a b means module a must be built before b. Output one valid comma-separated build order that builds all modules, or report a cycle. When multiple modules are buildable simultaneously pick the smallest-numbered module next. Treat duplicate dependency lines as a single dependency; any self-dependency indicates a cycle.
task: If possible print the build order as numbers separated by commas with no spaces (e.g. 1,2,3). If impossible print CYCLE exactly. Duplicate edges are ignored; self-loops cause CYCLE.
input_format:
Line 1: N M
Then M lines: a b (a before b).
constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 300000, 0 ≤ M ≤ 300000, 1 ≤ a,b ≤ N. Expected O(N+M) solution.

name: Task Unlock List — Report order or IMPOSSIBLE
background: There are N tasks (1..N). A line a b means task a unlocks task b (a must be done before b). Decide whether all tasks can be unlocked. If yes, print the unique deterministic order defined by always picking the smallest-numbered currently unlocked task. Ignore duplicate unlock lines; any self-unlock (a -> a) prevents completion.
task: If all tasks can be completed print their numbers in order separated by single spaces following the smallest-first tie rule. If not, print IMPOSSIBLE. Duplicate edges are ignored; self-loops make completion impossible.
input_format:
Line 1: N M
Next M lines: a b each meaning a before b.

name: Rival Teams
background: You have N people and some pairs are rivals. Every rivalry means the two people must be on opposing teams. A valid assignment gives each person either Team A or Team B. If a person has no rivals they may be on either team.
task: Decide whether a valid A/B assignment exists. If impossible print NO. If possible, produce one valid assignment using this deterministic rule: iterate vertices 1..N; when you find an unassigned vertex, start a BFS/DFS from that vertex (visit neighbours in increasing index order) and assign that starting vertex to Team A, propagating the opposite label along edges. Output NO or, if possible, first line YES and second line N tokens 'A' or 'B' (space-separated) giving the team for persons 1..N.
input_format: Line 1: two integers N M. Next M lines: two integers u v representing an undirected rivalry edge between u and v.
constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 200000, 0 ≤ M ≤ 200000, N+M ≤ 300000. Vertex indices 1..N. No more than two-team constraints; self-loop (u=u) means impossible because a vertex cannot be opposite itself.
test7_output:
YES
A B A B A B
test8_output:
YES
A B A B A

name: Same or Different Statements
background: You hear statements that two people are the same or different type. Each statement compares two people and claims either SAME or DIFFERENT. You must assign binary labels 0/1 to each person so all statements hold.
task: Decide if the statements are consistent. If inconsistent print CONTRADICTION. Otherwise print a single line with N integers (0 or 1) for persons 1..N. Use this deterministic tie-breaker: scan vertices 1..N, when encountering an unlabelled vertex assign it label 0 and propagate constraints, visiting neighbors in increasing index order.
input_format: Line 1: two integers N M. Next M lines: three integers u v t where t=0 means u and v must have the same label, and t=1 means they must have different labels.
constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 200000, 0 ≤ M ≤ 200000, N+M ≤ 300000. Vertex indices 1..N. Self-loop with t=1 is a contradiction; t=0 self-loop is allowed and means that vertex equals itself.

name: Two-Shift Schedule
background: Employees must be assigned to Day or Night shift. Some pairs cannot work the same shift and therefore must be assigned to opposite shifts. Employees without restrictions can be on either shift.
task: If a valid Day/Night assignment exists, output the number K of employees assigned to Day on the first line and on the second line the K indices in ascending order. If no valid assignment exists print NO. Tie-breaker: iterate vertices 1..N, when a vertex is unassigned start a BFS from it (visit neighbors in increasing index order) assigning that vertex to Day and propagating Night/Day on edges.
input_format: Line 1: two integers N M. Next M lines: two integers u v meaning u and v must be on opposite shifts.
constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 200000, 0 ≤ M ≤ 200000, N+M ≤ 300000. Vertex indices 1..N. Self-loop (u=u) disallows a valid assignment.

name: Alternating Components
background: Given an undirected graph where every edge insists the endpoints have opposite parity, each connected component can be split into two color classes. For each component we want the counts of the two classes.
task: If the graph is not bipartite (an edge forces a node to be opposite itself), print Not bipartite. Otherwise output the number C of connected components on the first line, then C lines each containing two integers a b: the count of vertices labeled 0 then 1 for that component. Use this deterministic tie-breaker: process vertices in increasing index order, when starting a component assign its smallest vertex label 0 and visit neighbours in increasing index order. List components in the output in order of their smallest vertex (increasing).
input_format: Line 1: two integers N M. Next M lines: two integers u v representing an undirected edge that requires opposite labels.
constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 200000, 0 ≤ M ≤ 200000, N+M ≤ 300000. Vertex indices 1..N. Self-loop implies Not bipartite.

name: Relationship Queries
background: You are given same/different constraints between people. First check consistency; if consistent, produce a deterministic 0/1 labeling (scan vertices 1..N, start each unlabelled vertex with 0, traverse neighbours in increasing order). Then answer queries asking if two people ended up the same or different.
task: Input N, M, Q. Next M lines: u v t (t=0 same, t=1 different). Next Q lines: u v queries. If constraints are inconsistent print INCONSISTENT and nothing else. Otherwise, after assigning labels by the deterministic rule, print Q lines each either SAME or DIFFERENT indicating whether the queried pair have equal labels.
input_format: Line 1: three integers N M Q. Next M lines: u v t as described. Next Q lines: u v queries.
constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 200000, 0 ≤ M,Q ≤ 200000, N+M+Q ≤ 300000. Vertex indices 1..N. Self-loop with t=1 is inconsistent; t=0 self-loop is allowed.

name: Teleport, Step, or Double
background: You stand on an integer position on a number line between 0 and 300000. From a value x you may move to x-1, x+1, or teleport to x*2 (staying inside the 0..300000 interval). Each move costs 1. The state-space (values) is implicit: you generate neighbours by those three rules.
task: Given start N and target K (0 ≤ N,K ≤ 300000), find the minimum number of moves to reach K from N. If N == K output 0. (There is always a path under these rules.)
input_format: Line 1: two integers N K
constraints: 0 ≤ N,K ≤ 300000. Allowed moves: x-1, x+1, x*2 (result must remain within 0..300000). Time limit expects O(range) BFS.

name: Reverse-and-Step Relay
background: You have integers between 0 and 300000. From x you may go to x-1, x+1, or to rev(x) where rev(x) is the decimal reversal of x (leading zeros are dropped, e.g. rev(120)=21). Each move costs 1.
task: Given start N and target K (0 ≤ N,K ≤ 300000), compute the minimum number of moves to reach K from N. If N==K output 0. (If multiple ways exist, just output the distance.)
input_format: Line 1: two integers N K
constraints: 0 ≤ N,K ≤ 300000. Moves: x-1, x+1, rev(x) (results must be within 0..300000). Use BFS over the implicit graph.

name: Add, Subtract, or Double (parameterized)
background: You manipulate integers in 0..300000. From x you can: add A (x+A), subtract B (x-B, allowed only if result ≥ 0), or double (x*2). Each operation costs 1. A and B are nonnegative integers provided in the input; subtraction by 0 is allowed (it produces the same state).
task: Given N, K, A, B find the minimum moves to reach K from N using those operations inside the 0..300000 interval. If K is unreachable output -1. If N==K output 0.
input_format: Line 1: four integers N K A B
constraints: 0 ≤ N,K ≤ 300000. 0 ≤ A,B ≤ 300000. Allowed moves: x+A, x-B (only if ≥0), x*2 (only if ≤300000). Answer must be the minimum number of unit-cost moves or -1 if unreachable.

name: Tripling with Path Output (lexicographic tiebreak)
background: You have values in 0..300000. From x you may move to x-1, x+1, or x*3 (result must stay within bounds). All moves cost 1. Besides the minimal moves count, we also want an actual shortest sequence of states starting with N and ending with K.
task: Given N and K (0 ≤ N,K ≤ 300000) output two lines: Line 1 is the minimum number of moves to go from N to K. Line 2 is one sequence of states (space-separated integers) of that minimum length, starting at N and ending at K. If multiple shortest sequences exist, output the lexicographically smallest sequence (compare sequences element-by-element). If N==K, output 0 and a single-number line with N.
input_format: Line 1: two integers N K
constraints: 0 ≤ N,K ≤ 300000. Moves: x-1, x+1, x*3 (results must be within 0..300000). Use BFS to find distances and reconstruct a path; among all shortest paths choose the lexicographically smallest sequence.

name: Parity Machine
background: You work on integers 0..300000 with a deterministic, parity-dependent rule: if x is even, you must replace x with x/2; if x is odd, you must replace x with x+5. There is exactly one possible move from any x (it must stay in bounds). Each move costs 1. Because every state has one successor inside 0..300000, the state evolution is a deterministic sequence (it may enter a cycle).
task: Given N and K (0 ≤ N,K ≤ 300000) find the minimum number of moves to reach K from N following the deterministic rule. If K is never reached (sequence enters a cycle without hitting K) output -1. If N==K output 0.
input_format: Line 1: two integers N K
constraints: 0 ≤ N,K ≤ 300000. Transition: if x is even -> x/2; else -> x+5 (result must be within 0..300000; if a step would go outside, it is not allowed and the process stops — treat as unreachable). Because the rule is deterministic there is at most one path; detect cycles or out-of-bounds and report -1 if K is not reached.

name: Midnight Heist
background: You are a thief in a straight street of houses. Each house has an integer amount of loot (can be positive, zero, or negative meaning a cost). You may rob any subset of houses but never two adjacent ones (robbing neighboring houses alerts the police). You may also choose to rob none.
task: Compute the maximum total loot you can obtain. If every choice would reduce your loot, you may choose to rob nobody and get 0. Output a single integer: the maximum achievable total.
input_format:
Line 1: n (number of houses)
Line 2: n space-separated integers a1..an (loot values)
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300000. Each ai is an integer with |ai| ≤ 10^9. Required time O(n), memory O(1) extra preferred.

name: Sunflower Harvest
background: A row of sunflower plots each yields an integer amount of seeds (can be negative meaning tending cost). You can harvest any nonadjacent plots. Unlike skipping completely, you must harvest at least one plot (the farm contract requires some output). If all plots reduce profit, you still must choose the single plot with the highest value (least loss).
task: Compute the maximum total seeds obtainable by selecting a nonadjacent subset of plots with the constraint you must select at least one plot. Output the maximum total as a single integer.
input_format:
Line 1: n (number of plots)
Line 2: n space-separated integers v1..vn (yield values)
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300000. Each vi is an integer with |vi| ≤ 10^9. Expected O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.

name: Prize Stalls
background: Along a row of stalls are prizes with integer values (can be negative). You can claim prizes from nonadjacent stalls. You are allowed to claim none (yield 0). Among all ways that achieve the maximum total prize value, you want the fewest stalls claimed (smaller teams are cheaper).
task: Output two integers: the maximum total prize, and the minimal number of stalls required to achieve that maximum. If the best choice is to claim none, the output should be "0 0".
input_format:
Line 1: n (number of stalls)
Line 2: n space-separated integers p1..pn (prize values)
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300000. Each pi is integer with |pi| ≤ 10^9. Expected O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.

name: Buffer Allocation
background: A line of memory slots each has an integer benefit if allocated (negative means it costs more than it helps). You may allocate slots but never two adjacent ones. Additionally, you are only allowed to allocate slots with nonnegative benefit (zeros or positives). If there are no nonnegative slots at all, allocation is impossible.
task: If at least one slot is nonnegative, compute the maximum total benefit achievable by selecting nonadjacent slots among only nonnegative slots, and print that integer. If no slot is nonnegative, print IMPOSSIBLE (all caps).
input_format:
Line 1: n (number of slots)
Line 2: n space-separated integers b1..bn (benefits)
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300000. Each bi is integer with |bi| ≤ 10^9. Expect O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.

name: Festival Seating
background: VIPs are seated along a single row: each seat has an integer enjoyment value (may be negative). You must seat at least one VIP. No two seated VIPs can sit in adjacent seats. Among all seating choices that reach the maximum total enjoyment, output the lexicographically smallest list of chosen seat indices (1-based). Lexicographic comparison treats the lists as sequences compared elementwise; shorter prefixes win if identical to that point.
task: First print the maximum total enjoyment (single integer). On the next line, print the chosen seat indices in increasing order separated by single spaces (1-based). You must choose at least one seat; if multiple selections tie on sum, output the lexicographically smallest index list.
input_format:
Line 1: n (number of seats)
Line 2: n space-separated integers s1..sn (enjoyment values)
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300000. Each si is integer with |si| ≤ 10^9. Expected O(n) time; reconstruction of one optimal set should be O(n).

name: Staircase Toll
background: You climb a staircase of n steps. Each step i (1..n) has a toll cost. You start before step 1 (position 0) with cost 0. From any position you may move forward by 1 or 2 steps. Some steps may be blocked (cost -1) and cannot be landed on.
task: Compute the minimum total toll to land exactly on step n. If step n cannot be reached under the rules, output -1. Tie-breaking is irrelevant — just report the minimum cost.
input_format:
Line 1: n
Line 2: n integers cost[1] ... cost[n] (use -1 for blocked steps)
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300000. Each cost[i] is either -1 or 0 ≤ cost[i] ≤ 10^9. Time: O(n) expected.

name: Frog Heights
background: A frog stands on stone 1 of n stones in a line. Each stone i has height h[i]. The frog can jump from stone i to i+1 or i+2. The energy cost of a jump i→j is |h[i]−h[j]|. The frog starts on stone 1 and wants to reach stone n.
task: Output the minimum total energy required to reach stone n. If n=1 output 0.
input_format:
Line 1: n
Line 2: n integers h[1] ... h[n]
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300000. Each h[i] is an integer with |h[i]| ≤ 10^9. Time: O(n).

name: Required Checkpoints
background: Steps 1..n have costs; you start at position 0 (cost 0). You can jump forward by 1 or 2 steps and may not land on blocked steps (cost -1). You are given a list of checkpoints (positions). You must visit them in the exact order given. The journey ends at the last checkpoint; if the list is empty, you must end at step n.
task: Find the minimum total cost to perform a sequence of moves that visits the given checkpoints in order and finishes at the final required position. If any required visit is impossible, output -1. Visiting the same checkpoint twice in a row (repeated position in input) requires no movement and adds no cost.
input_format:
Line 1: n k
Line 2: n integers cost[1] ... cost[n] (-1 for blocked)
Line 3: k integers p[1] ... p[k] (positions to visit in the given order). If k=0 the third line is omitted.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300000. 0 ≤ k ≤ n. Each cost[i] is -1 or 0 ≤ cost[i] ≤ 10^9. All 1 ≤ p[j] ≤ n. Time: O(n).

name: Choose Start Step
background: You must land exactly on step n. Each step i has cost[i] (−1 means blocked). Before moving you may choose to start already standing on step 1 or on step 2 (if that position exists and is not blocked). When you start on a step you immediately pay that step's cost. From any landed position you may move forward by 1 or 2 steps. If both starting choices are possible, pick the one that yields smaller total cost; if costs tie, prefer starting at step 1.
task: Output two values: the minimum total cost and the chosen starting step (1 or 2). If no valid plan exists (neither start leads to step n), output -1 on a single line.
input_format:
Line 1: n
Line 2: n integers cost[1] ... cost[n] (-1 for blocked)
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300000. Each cost[i] is -1 or 0 ≤ cost[i] ≤ 10^9. Time: O(n).

name: Two-step Penalty Frog
background: A frog stands on stone 1 and needs to reach stone n. Stone i has height h[i]. The frog can jump from i to i+1 or i+2. The cost of a jump i→j is |h[i]−h[j]| plus an extra penalty P whenever the jump length is 2 (the penalty applies for each such jump).
task: Output the minimum total cost to reach stone n. If n=1 output 0.
input_format:
Line 1: n P
Line 2: n integers h[1] ... h[n]
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300000. 0 ≤ P ≤ 10^9. Each h[i] is integer with |h[i]| ≤ 10^9. Time: O(n).

name: Classic Alphabet Decode
background: You have a string of decimal digits representing a sequence of tokens. A single-digit token is any digit '1'..'9' (the digit '0' is not a valid single token). A two-digit token is any two-digit number between 10 and 26 inclusive (its first digit cannot be '0'). You must count how many different ways the input string can be partitioned into valid tokens (each token is either one digit or two adjacent digits). Return the count modulo a given modulus.
task: Given a digit string s and an integer modulus m, compute the number of valid partitions of s into single- or two-digit tokens under the rules above. If there are no valid partitions output 0. Always reduce the final count modulo m (0 <= answer < m).
input_format:
Line 1: a non-empty digit string s (length up to 100000)
Line 2: integer m (1 <= m <= 10^9+7)
constraints: 1 <= |s| <= 100000. s contains only characters '0'..'9'. Single digit tokens allowed only for '1'..'9'. Two-digit tokens allowed only if the two-digit integer is between 10 and 26 inclusive. Time O(n).

name: Packet Size Segments
background: Interpret the digit string as adjacent packet descriptors. A single-digit packet is any digit '1'..'9' (not '0'). A two-digit packet is any two-digit number between 10 and 34 inclusive (first digit cannot be '0'). Count how many segmentations of the string into such packets exist, modulo m.
task: Given digit string s and modulus m, output the count of valid segmentations into single-digit packets (1..9) or two-digit packets (10..34). If no segmentation is valid output 0. Return answer modulo m (0 <= answer < m).
input_format:
Line 1: digit string s
Line 2: integer m
constraints: 1 <= |s| <= 100000. s only '0'..'9'. Single-digit packets allowed only for '1'..'9'. Two-digit packets allowed only for integers between 10 and 34 inclusive. Time O(n).

name: Zero-Permissive 50-75 Codes
background: Here single-digit tokens may be any digit '0'..'9' (so '0' is allowed alone). Two-digit tokens are allowed only when the two-digit number is between 50 and 75 inclusive (so the first digit must be '5','6', or '7'). Count how many ways the string can be split into tokens (single-digit or allowed two-digit), modulo m.
task: Given digit string s and modulus m, compute the number of valid tokenizations where single digits '0'..'9' are always valid single tokens and two-digit tokens are valid only if their numeric value is between 50 and 75 inclusive. Output 0 if no tokenization exists. Return answer modulo m.
input_format:
Line 1: digit string s
Line 2: integer m
constraints: 1 <= |s| <= 100000. s only contains '0'..'9'. Single-digit tokens allowed for any digit 0..9. Two-digit tokens allowed only for integers 50..75 inclusive. Time O(n).

name: Exactly-k Two-Digits
background: Tokens follow the classic rule: single-digit tokens are '1'..'9' (no single '0'), two-digit tokens are integers 10..26 (first digit not '0'). In addition, you must use exactly k two-digit tokens in the partition.
task: Given digit string s, integer k, and modulus m, count partitions of s into valid tokens (single or two-digit as above) that use exactly k two-digit tokens. If none exist output 0. Return the count modulo m (0 <= answer < m).
input_format:
Line 1: digit string s
Line 2: integers k m (0 <= k <= |s|)
constraints: 1 <= |s| <= 100000. s is digits '0'..'9'. Single-digit tokens allowed only for '1'..'9'. Two-digit tokens allowed only for integers 10..26 inclusive. 0 <= k <= |s|. Time O(n*k) expected (k up to n).

name: No Adjacent Two-Digits
background: Standard tokens: single-digit tokens are '1'..'9' (no single '0'), two-digit tokens are integers 10..26 inclusive. Additionally, two two-digit tokens may not be adjacent in the partition — after a two-digit token there must be at least one single-digit token before another two-digit token.
task: Given digit string s and modulus m, count partitions into valid tokens that never place two two-digit tokens back-to-back. If no valid partitions exist output 0. Return the count modulo m.
input_format:
Line 1: digit string s
Line 2: integer m
constraints: 1 <= |s| <= 100000. s only '0'..'9'. Single-digit tokens allowed only for '1'..'9'. Two-digit tokens allowed only for integers 10..26 inclusive. Two-digit tokens are not allowed to appear consecutively in the chosen partition. Time O(n).

name: Exact Coupon Target
background: You have a collection of nonnegative coupons (each can be used at most once). A subset sum is the total value when you pick some coupons. Empty subset (picking none) yields sum 0. Determine whether you can pick a subset whose total equals a specified target.
task: Decide if some subset of the given n values sums exactly to target T. If yes print YES; otherwise print NO.
input_format:
Line 1: n T
Line 2: n space-separated integers a1 a2 ... an
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200; 0 ≤ ai ≤ 20000; 0 ≤ T ≤ 20000. Each ai may be zero; no negative values.

name: Cap-Max Subset
background: Given nonnegative item values (each usable at most once) and a capacity cap C, we want the largest achievable total that does not exceed C. The empty selection yields 0.
task: Output a single integer: the maximum subset sum ≤ C that can be formed. The empty subset (sum 0) is always allowed.
input_format:

Line 2: n space-separated integers a1 a2 ... an

name: Top-Up to Target
